fields.title: Postmortem That Changes the System
fields.keyTakeaway: A useful postmortem measures time-to-detect separately from time-to-recover and asks not "what broke", but "why did this lead to such consequences".
fields.sections/0/blocks/0/text: The incident is over. How to make sure it doesn't happen again, and why does it usually repeat?
fields.sections/1/blocks/0/text: A post-mortem ending in a list of tasks without owners is a ritual. Three cascades in half a year in `SC1-G-B` are a direct consequence of reviews after which a specific call was fixed without asking the question about the class of the problem.
fields.sections/2/blocks/0/text: A [[postmortem|postmortem]] is a document and discussion after an incident. A useful one contains five parts.
fields.sections/2/blocks/1/text: **Timeline with timestamps.** When it started, when it was detected, when it was understood, when it was fixed. This gives two metrics: [[time-to-detect|time to detect]] and [[time-to-recover|time to recover]]. The first one is often larger than the second, and that is a separate finding.
fields.sections/2/blocks/2/text: **Impact in product terms.** Not "22 minutes downtime", but "980 lost orders, 2.3M revenue, 31 minutes of error budget".
fields.sections/2/blocks/3/text: **Cause and, separately, scale factors.** The root cause is usually minor. The question "why did this lead to a total stop" is more important than "what broke".
fields.sections/2/blocks/4/text: **What worked.** Not just failures: if degradation worked, it needs to be recorded, otherwise people will stop maintaining it.
fields.sections/2/blocks/5/text: **Actions with owners and deadlines.** Each one specific, with a name and date.
fields.sections/2/blocks/6/text: A [[blameless-postmortem|blameless postmortem]] is not politeness, but a condition for reliability. Where culprits are sought, details are hidden, and the review becomes useless.
fields.sections/2/blocks/7/text: The practice that distinguishes working postmortems from ritual ones: **asking about the class, not the instance.** Not "why did reviews go down", but "why is any slow service able to stop the product". The first gives a task for a day, the second for three weeks and closes future incidents.
fields.sections/3/blocks/1/text: *Chronology:* slowdown from 19:31, detected at 19:49 from complaints, cause understood at 20:02. Time to detect — 18 minutes, time to recover — 13.
fields.sections/3/blocks/2/text: The main finding was right here: detection longer than recovery, and the slowdown graph was visible from 19:31. The problem wasn't in fixing it, but in the fact that nobody was looking.
fields.sections/3/blocks/3/text: *Impact:* 980 orders, 31 minutes of budget out of 43.
fields.sections/3/blocks/4/text: *Cause:* index rebuild. *Scale factor:* lack of timeouts on inter-service calls.
fields.sections/3/blocks/5/text: *What worked:* checkout kept working for those already on screen.
fields.sections/3/blocks/6/text: *Actions:* alerts on all services — on-call, 3 days. Timeouts and cutoffs — tech lead, 3 weeks. Ratings cache — catalog team, 3 days. Communication templates — product manager, 2 days.
fields.sections/3/blocks/7/text: The key difference from the previous two reviews was that the class question was asked, and a three-week task appeared instead of a one-day one.
fields.sections/4/blocks/0/text: Reviewing every minor glitch is a waste of time. The threshold is defined in advance, but once a quarter it is useful to review minor incidents together: often they add up to a single pattern.
fields.sections/5/blocks/0/text: A useful postmortem measures time-to-detect separately from time-to-recover and asks not "what broke", but "why did this lead to such consequences".
